newsitem.title: USA: Budget agency says U.S. deficit picture brighter.
newsitem.headline: Budget agency says U.S. deficit picture brighter.

text.p: The Congressional Budget Office Monday lowered by one-third its forecast for the budget deficit but warned that red ink will run near $200 billion by 2002 if the White House and Congress take no action.

The non-partisan budget analysis arm of Congress said this year's federal deficit is predicted to reach $124 billion, far less than the $171 billion it projected a year ago. At that time it also forecast the deficit in 2002 at $285 billion but now sees that figure at $188 billion.

CBO director June O'Neill credited enactment of welfare reform, slower growth in health care costs, larger tax revenues and lower interest on the federal debt for leading to the improvements in the deficit outlook.
Last year also ended up better than the CBO forecast, with a deficit of $107 billion in 1996 versus $116 billion forecast in May.

O'Neill said in an accompanying statement that it would be much less painful if action is taken now than it would be if Washington waits to deal with the deficit until the next century, when the baby-boom generation enters retirement.

"Taking action now would contribute to assuring budgetary stability in the next century, particularly if the policy changes adopted deal with the problems associated with federal health care and other retirement benefits," she said.
The White House and congressional leaders of both parties have spoken optimistically this year of the chances of reaching an agreement to balance the budget by 2002.

If they succeed, the CBO said the economy would feel a boost, helping them along in their task. Only $154 billion of deficit reduction -- either spending cuts or tax increases -- would be needed in 2002 to bring the budget into balance.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry called the chances of an agreement "excellent," and said, "I think it's certainly within the realm of the possible that the Republican Congress and the Democrat president could come to agreement quickly and get the job done."

President Bill Clinton is to send his fiscal 1998 budget to Congress Feb. 6. Republican leaders have said they consider his proposals to be the opening offer in the budget negotiations and have emphasized that much of his plan has parallels in their own proposals.

Both favor capital gains tax relief, although Republicans want broad cuts and Clinton is seeking a targeted cut for homesellers. Both include a $500 per child tax credit. And, one of the most controversial of Clinton's plans -- a $138 billion reduction in spending for Medicare health care -- has met guarded support from Republicans.
Senate Budget Committee staff director Bill Hoagland told reporters informal talks on the budget would begin even before Clinton's plan is unveiled.

Hoagland said the deficit problem would make it difficult to cut spending, and could possibly make necessary a freeze on discretionary programs -- those agencies that handle education, housing, national parks, transportation and other programs where spending is approved annually.
O'Neill agreed that cutting annual spending will be tough. "Wringing savings out of (domestic) discretionary programs is becoming harder and harder," she said.

In another piece of good news for the budget negotiators, CBO said it sees no signs for an end to the U.S. economic expansion. A downturn in the economy would worsen the deficit. Revenues would fall, more people would seek government assistance and it would become harder to cut spending or raise taxes.

While some in Congress have criticized the 2.2 percent economic growth rate as too low, continued moderate growth and low inflation are the forecast for up to two years. The CBO's preliminary economic forecast made available in December showed the same.
